description: Map every stakeholder by influence and interest using the power-interest grid. Design communication frequency, channel, and message depth for each quadrant. High-power/high-interest stakeholders get frequent, detailed updates. Low-power/low-interest get periodic summaries. Works for projects, organizations, and personal networks.

steps.description: Identify every stakeholder: anyone who affects or is affected by the outcome.

inputs.name: initiative-description
inputs.desc: What is being communicated about (a project, an organization, a change, a product)

outputs.name: stakeholder-list
outputs.desc: Every stakeholder with their role, relationship to the initiative, and what they care about

outputs.name: hidden-stakeholders
outputs.desc: Stakeholders who are not obvious but will be affected (downstream users, regulators, competitors, support teams)

process: List the obvious stakeholders: the sponsor, the team, the end users, the manager, the customers.
Walk the impact chain: who is affected by the output? Who is affected by the process? Who is affected by the resource consumption? Who will be asked to change their behavior?

Identify the hidden stakeholders: the team whose roadmap shifts because of this initiative, the support team that will handle questions, the compliance team that needs to approve, the competitor who will respond.
For each stakeholder, note what they care about: outcomes, timeline, cost, quality, process, recognition, risk.

steps.description: Place each stakeholder on the power-interest grid: high power/high interest (manage closely), high power/low interest (keep satisfied), low power/high interest (keep informed), low power/low interest (monitor).

inputs.name: stakeholder-list
inputs.desc: The full stakeholder list with roles and concerns

outputs.name: power-interest-grid
outputs.desc: Each stakeholder placed in one of four quadrants with their power score (1-5) and interest score (1-5)

outputs.name: quadrant-strategies
outputs.desc: The communication strategy for each quadrant: frequency, channel, message depth, and escalation protocol

process: Rate each stakeholder's power (1-5): their ability to help or block the initiative. A senior executive with budget authority is a 5. A downstream user with no decision-making role is a 1.
Rate each stakeholder's interest (1-5): how much they care about the initiative's outcome. Someone whose daily work changes is a 5. Someone who is tangentially aware is a 1.

Place each stakeholder in the grid. Manage closely (high/high): frequent two-way communication, involve in decisions. Keep satisfied (high/low): periodic updates, no surprises. Keep informed (low/high): regular updates, listen to concerns. Monitor (low/low): periodic summaries.

Check for misalignment: a stakeholder you are treating as low-interest who is actually high-interest will feel ignored. A low-power stakeholder you are treating as high-power will consume disproportionate time.

steps.description: Write the communication plan: for each stakeholder or group, define what they receive, how often, through what channel, and who owns the communication.

inputs.name: power-interest-grid
inputs.desc: The stakeholder grid with quadrant strategies

inputs.name: quadrant-strategies
inputs.desc: The communication approach for each quadrant

outputs.name: communication-plan
outputs.desc: For each stakeholder or group: the message type, frequency, channel, owner, and the escalation trigger

outputs.name: communication-calendar
outputs.desc: A calendar of all planned communications with dates, audiences, and owners

process: For manage-closely stakeholders: weekly or bi-weekly face-to-face (or video) updates. Involve them in decisions before they are made. Share problems early, not after they are resolved.
For keep-satisfied stakeholders: monthly written summaries. Highlight outcomes, not process. Flag anything that might concern them before it becomes a surprise.
For keep-informed stakeholders: bi-weekly email or newsletter. Share progress, answer questions, and acknowledge their input. They are your advocates if treated well.
For monitor stakeholders: quarterly summary or inclusion in broader organizational updates. No special communication unless something changes their power or interest.

steps.description: Review the stakeholder map when the context changes. Stakeholders move between quadrants as power and interest shift.

outputs.name: updated-grid
outputs.desc: The revised stakeholder grid with any movements noted

outputs.name: plan-adjustments
outputs.desc: Changes to the communication plan based on stakeholder movements

process: At each major milestone or context change, re-rate each stakeholder's power and interest. Has anyone gained or lost influence? Has anyone become more or less interested?
Move stakeholders between quadrants as needed. A previously low-interest executive who is now being asked to fund the next phase moves to high-interest.
Adjust the communication plan to match the new grid. A stakeholder who moved to manage-closely needs more frequent, more detailed communication immediately.
Look for new stakeholders who emerged since the last review. Add them to the grid and the plan.

description: Structure messages using the Minto Pyramid principle: start with the conclusion, then the supporting arguments, then the evidence. The reader gets the answer first and can stop reading when they have enough. Applies to emails, reports, presentations, proposals, and any communication longer than two sentences.

steps.description: Write the conclusion first. This is the single sentence that answers the reader's question or states the recommendation.

inputs.name: communication-purpose
inputs.desc: What this communication needs to accomplish (inform, persuade, request, decide)

inputs.name: audience
inputs.desc: Who is reading and what they care about

inputs.name: key-information
inputs.desc: The information, analysis, or recommendation to communicate

outputs.name: conclusion-statement
outputs.desc: The single sentence that the entire communication supports. If the reader reads only this sentence, they know the answer.

outputs.name: audience-question
outputs.desc: The question in the reader's mind that this communication answers

process: Identify the question in the reader's mind. A status update answers 'are we on track?' A proposal answers 'should we do this?' A report answers 'what happened and what does it mean?'
Write the answer to that question in one sentence. This is the conclusion. It goes first, not last.
Test the conclusion: if the reader reads only this sentence and nothing else, do they know the answer? If not, sharpen it.
The conclusion is not a summary of the communication. It is the answer. 'This report covers three areas' is a summary. 'We should expand to the European market in Q3' is a conclusion.

steps.description: Build 2-4 supporting arguments that hold up the conclusion. Each argument is a reason to believe the conclusion.

outputs.name: supporting-arguments
outputs.desc: 2-4 arguments, each stated in one sentence, that support the conclusion. Together they are sufficient; individually they are necessary.

outputs.name: argument-order
outputs.desc: The order of arguments: strongest first if persuading, most important first if informing

process: Ask: why should the reader believe the conclusion? List every reason.
Group the reasons into 2-4 categories. Each category becomes a supporting argument. More than 4 arguments means the categories are too granular.
State each argument in one sentence. Like the conclusion, each argument should stand on its own as a claim.

Order the arguments: if the purpose is persuasion, lead with the strongest argument. If the purpose is information, lead with the most important argument. If the purpose is a decision, lead with the argument that addresses the reader's biggest concern.

steps.description: Under each argument, place the evidence that supports it. Data, examples, and citations. The reader drills into the evidence only if they question the argument.

inputs.name: supporting-arguments
inputs.desc: The arguments to back with evidence

outputs.name: evidence-structure
outputs.desc: Under each argument: the data points, examples, and citations that support it. Organized so the reader can scan or deep-dive.

outputs.name: complete-message-structure
outputs.desc: The full pyramid: conclusion, arguments, evidence, ready to draft into the final format

process: For each argument, list the evidence: data points, examples, precedents, expert opinions, test results. Each piece of evidence should directly support the argument it sits under.
Remove evidence that does not support any argument. Interesting but irrelevant data weakens the structure.
For each evidence item, assess its strength: primary data (strong), secondary analysis (moderate), anecdote (weak). Lead with the strongest evidence.
The reader should be able to read at three levels: conclusion only (10 seconds), conclusion plus arguments (1 minute), full document with evidence (5+ minutes). Each level is self-contained.

steps.description: Adapt the pyramid structure to the specific format: email, presentation, report, or conversation.

outputs.name: formatted-message
outputs.desc: The message adapted to the target format with the pyramid structure intact

outputs.name: format-notes
outputs.desc: Format-specific adaptations: email subject line = conclusion, slide title = argument, appendix = evidence

process: For email: subject line states the conclusion or action needed. First sentence restates it. Bullet points for arguments. Evidence in attachments or linked documents.
For presentations: slide title = argument. Slide body = evidence. First slide = conclusion. Last slide = conclusion restated with the ask.
For reports: executive summary = conclusion plus arguments. Body sections = one argument per section with evidence. Appendix = detailed data.
For conversations: state the conclusion first. Pause for reaction. If the listener agrees, stop. If they question, give the relevant argument and evidence.

description: Design a feedback system that produces actionable change, not empty surveys. Uses the SBI (Situation-Behavior-Impact) framework for specificity. Feedback that does not name a specific behavior and a specific impact is not actionable. Works for manager-to-report, peer-to-peer, customer-to-company, and self-assessment.

steps.description: Define what the feedback system must accomplish. Most feedback systems fail because they try to do everything (measure, motivate, develop, rank) with one instrument.

inputs.name: context
inputs.desc: Where the feedback system will operate (a team, a company, a classroom, a personal relationship, a product)

inputs.name: desired-outcomes
inputs.desc: What should change as a result of the feedback (behavior change, skill development, product improvement, relationship improvement)

outputs.name: feedback-purpose
outputs.desc: The single primary purpose of the feedback system and the secondary purposes it must also serve

outputs.name: feedback-scope
outputs.desc: What is in scope (specific behaviors and their impacts) and what is out of scope (personality, intent, permanent traits)

process: Define the primary purpose: is this feedback for development (helping someone improve), evaluation (measuring performance), recognition (acknowledging contribution), or course correction (stopping a problem)?

Define the scope: feedback addresses behaviors and their impacts, not personality traits or intentions. 'You arrived late to the last three client meetings' is in scope. 'You are unprofessional' is out of scope.
Identify the feedback loops: who gives feedback to whom, how often, and through what channel?
Define what success looks like: the feedback system is working when recipients change specific behaviors in response to specific feedback, measurably.

steps.description: Train the feedback givers on the SBI framework: Situation (when and where), Behavior (what specifically happened), Impact (the measurable effect).

inputs.name: feedback-purpose
inputs.desc: The purpose and scope of the feedback system

outputs.name: sbi-guide
outputs.desc: The SBI framework guide: how to structure feedback as Situation-Behavior-Impact with examples for the specific context

outputs.name: common-mistakes
outputs.desc: The mistakes to avoid: vague feedback, personality feedback, feedback without impact, delayed feedback, public negative feedback

process: Teach the Situation: describe when and where the behavior occurred. 'In yesterday's team meeting' or 'On the customer call last Tuesday.' Specificity prevents the recipient from dismissing the feedback as general.

Teach the Behavior: describe what the person did, not what you think they intended. 'You interrupted the client twice during their explanation' not 'You were rude to the client.' Observable behavior, not inferred motivation.

Teach the Impact: describe the measurable effect. 'The client stopped sharing details and the meeting ended 15 minutes early without a decision' not 'It was bad.' Impact makes feedback actionable because it ties behavior to consequence.
Provide examples for the specific context. For a product feedback system, SBI becomes: Situation (the use case), Behavior (what the product did), Impact (the effect on the user's workflow).

steps.description: Design the collection mechanism: how feedback is gathered, when, and from whom.

inputs.name: feedback-scope
inputs.desc: What is in and out of scope

outputs.name: collection-design
outputs.desc: The feedback collection process: trigger events (after a meeting, after a sprint, after a customer interaction), the collection method (form, conversation, retrospective), and the storage

outputs.name: frequency-and-timing
outputs.desc: When feedback is collected: event-triggered (within 48 hours of the behavior) vs. periodic (weekly, monthly). Event-triggered is more accurate.

process: Define the trigger events: what prompts feedback collection? After a client meeting, after a sprint, after a product release, after a significant interaction. Event-triggered feedback is more specific than calendar-triggered.

Design the collection form: three fields matching SBI: 'Describe the situation (when and where),' 'Describe the specific behavior (what happened),' 'Describe the impact (what was the effect).' Reject entries that skip any field.
Set the timing: feedback collected within 48 hours of the behavior is accurate. Feedback collected at the end of the quarter is a popularity contest based on recency.
Define who provides feedback to whom: direct reports to managers, peers to peers, customers to the team, self-assessment. 360-degree feedback uses all four.

steps.description: Convert feedback into action. This is where most feedback systems fail. Feedback that is collected but not acted on trains people to ignore the system.

inputs.name: feedback-purpose
inputs.desc: The primary purpose of the system

outputs.name: action-conversion-process
outputs.desc: How feedback is turned into specific actions: behavior change commitments with deadlines, skill development plans, product changes, or process improvements

outputs.name: feedback-effectiveness-metrics
outputs.desc: How to measure whether the feedback system is working: behavior change rate, action completion rate, and recipient satisfaction with feedback quality

process: For each piece of feedback, the recipient (or the responsible party) must respond with an action: 'I will [specific behavior change] starting [date]' or 'We will [product change] by [date]' or 'Noted, no action needed because [reason].'
Track the actions: did the behavior change? Did the product change ship? If actions are not tracked, the system degrades to a suggestion box.

Measure the system's effectiveness: what percentage of feedback resulted in a measurable action? What percentage of actions were completed? What is the recipient's rating of feedback quality (specific and actionable vs. vague and unhelpful)?

Review the system quarterly: is the feedback getting more specific over time (SBI training is working)? Are actions being completed (accountability is working)? Are the desired outcomes changing (the system is producing results)?

description: Navigate difficult conversations using the interest-based approach from the Harvard Negotiation Project. Separate the person from the problem. Focus on interests, not positions. Generate options before deciding. Use objective criteria. Works for performance conversations, conflict resolution, salary discussions, relationship issues, and complaints.

steps.description: Prepare before the conversation. Most difficult conversations go badly because people enter them without preparation, driven by emotion rather than structure.

inputs.name: situation-description
inputs.desc: What happened and why this conversation is needed

inputs.name: desired-outcome
inputs.desc: What you want to be true after the conversation that is not true now

outputs.name: your-interests
outputs.desc: Your underlying interests (not your position): what you actually need, why you need it, and what flexibility you have

outputs.name: their-likely-interests
outputs.desc: Your best estimate of the other person's interests: what they need, why, and what flexibility they might have

outputs.name: preparation-notes
outputs.desc: The facts (what happened, observable behavior, measurable impact), your interests, their likely interests, and options you could propose

process: Write down the facts: what specific, observable events occurred? Strip out interpretation and emotion. 'You missed the deadline by 5 days' is a fact. 'You do not care about deadlines' is an interpretation.

Identify your interests (not your position). Your position is what you want ('I want you to apologize'). Your interest is why you want it ('I need to know this will not happen again because it affects the client relationship'). Interests have more room for creative solutions than positions.

Estimate their interests: what are they likely concerned about? What constraints are they operating under? What do they need from you? If you cannot imagine their perspective, you are not ready for the conversation.
Draft 2-3 possible options that address both sets of interests. Enter the conversation with options, not demands.

steps.description: Open the conversation by stating the purpose, acknowledging both perspectives, and inviting their view first.

inputs.name: preparation-notes
inputs.desc: The prepared facts, interests, and options

inputs.name: desired-outcome
inputs.desc: What you want to be true after the conversation

outputs.name: opening-script
outputs.desc: The first three sentences of the conversation: the purpose, the acknowledgment of complexity, and the invitation to share their perspective

outputs.name: ground-rules
outputs.desc: The ground rules for the conversation: no interrupting, focus on interests, no attribution of motive

process: State the purpose neutrally: 'I want to talk about [the situation] because [it matters to the relationship/project/team]. I have some observations and I want to hear your perspective too.'
Acknowledge the complexity: 'I recognize this is not simple and there may be things I do not see.' This is not weakness; it is accuracy. You do not have the full picture.

Invite their view first: 'Before I share my perspective, I would like to hear yours. What happened from your side?' Listening first accomplishes two things: you learn information you did not have, and the other person feels heard (which makes them more receptive).
Set the ground rule: 'I would like us to focus on what we both need and what we can do going forward, not on assigning blame.'

steps.description: Explore interests beneath positions. When the other person states a position, ask why it matters to them. Beneath every position is an interest that can be met in multiple ways.

inputs.name: their-likely-interests
inputs.desc: Your estimate of their interests, to be updated during the conversation

outputs.name: shared-interests
outputs.desc: Interests that both parties share (these are the foundation for agreement)

outputs.name: different-but-compatible-interests
outputs.desc: Interests that differ but do not conflict (these allow creative trades)

outputs.name: conflicting-interests
outputs.desc: Interests that genuinely conflict (these require compromise or objective criteria)

process: When they state a position, ask 'Why is that important to you?' or 'What would that give you?' to uncover the interest beneath the position.
When you state your interest, explain why: 'I need [interest] because [reason].' The reason helps the other person understand what would satisfy you, not just what you are demanding.

Sort the interests into three categories: shared (you both want the project to succeed), different but compatible (you want credit and they want learning: both achievable), and conflicting (you both want the same limited resource).

For shared interests, acknowledge them explicitly: 'We both want [shared interest]. That is our common ground.' For conflicting interests, do not pretend they do not exist. Name them and address them next.

steps.description: Generate options that address both sets of interests. The best option is one that satisfies your top interest and their top interest simultaneously.

outputs.name: option-list
outputs.desc: 3-5 options that address both parties' interests, ranging from your ideal to a fair compromise

outputs.name: evaluation-criteria
outputs.desc: Objective criteria for choosing between options: fairness, precedent, market value, expert opinion, or mutual satisfaction

process: Brainstorm options without evaluating them. Generate at least 5 possibilities, including creative ones. 'What if we...' is the opening for each option.
For each option, check: does it address your top interest? Does it address their top interest? If an option addresses both, it is a strong candidate.

Where interests conflict and no option addresses both, propose objective criteria: 'Let us use [market rate / industry standard / past precedent / expert opinion] to decide this, rather than either of us imposing our preference.'
Present the options as a menu, not as a take-it-or-leave-it proposal. 'Here are three approaches I see. What are your thoughts? Do you see an option I am missing?'

steps.description: Close the conversation with a specific agreement and follow-through plan. A conversation without an agreement is a discussion. An agreement without follow-through is fiction.

outputs.name: agreement-record
outputs.desc: The specific agreement: what each party will do, by when, and how success will be measured

outputs.name: follow-up-plan
outputs.desc: The follow-up: when will you check in on the agreement, and what happens if it is not being followed

process: Select the option or combine elements from multiple options. Confirm agreement by restating it: 'So we are agreeing that [person A will do X by date Y] and [person B will do Z by date W]. Is that right?'
Write down the agreement. Verbal agreements are forgotten or remembered differently. Even an email summary sent within 24 hours is better than memory.
Set the follow-up: 'Let us check in on [date] to see how this is going.' The follow-up is not optional. Without it, the agreement degrades.

If the conversation did not produce an agreement, acknowledge it honestly: 'We did not reach agreement today. Here is what I heard. Let us schedule another conversation for [date] after we have both had time to think.' An honest non-agreement is better than a false agreement.

description: Design status reports that surface problems early instead of hiding them. Exception-based reporting: report what changed, what is blocked, and what needs a decision. If everything is on track, the report is one sentence. Most status reports are long because they describe activity, not outcomes.

steps.description: Design the status report structure: what is reported, in what order, and at what frequency.

inputs.name: audience
inputs.desc: Who reads the status report and what decisions they make from it

inputs.name: initiative-description
inputs.desc: What is being reported on (a project, a team, an operation, a personal goal)

outputs.name: report-structure
outputs.desc: The report template: headline status (green/yellow/red), exceptions (what changed, what is blocked, what needs a decision), metrics (3-5 key measures), and upcoming milestones

outputs.name: reporting-frequency
outputs.desc: How often the report is sent, based on the rate of change and the audience's decision cadence

process: Define the headline status: green (on track, no action needed), yellow (at risk, action may be needed), red (off track, action needed now). The reader should know the overall state in one glance.

Define the exception section: what changed since the last report? What is blocked and needs help? What decisions need to be made by the reader? This is the section that matters. If there are no exceptions, the report is: 'Green. No exceptions. Next milestone: [date].'
Define the metrics: 3-5 numbers that the reader can track over time. Choose metrics that are leading (predict future state) not lagging (report past state).
Set the frequency: match it to the audience's decision cadence. If they make weekly decisions, report weekly. If they review monthly, report monthly. More frequent than the decision cadence is noise.

steps.description: Train the reporters to write exceptions that are actionable: what happened, what is the impact, what is needed.

inputs.name: audience
inputs.desc: Who reads and what they need to do

outputs.name: exception-writing-guide
outputs.desc: How to write an exception: the fact (what changed), the impact (what is affected), the ask (what is needed from the reader), and the deadline

outputs.name: exception-examples
outputs.desc: Examples of good exceptions (specific, actionable) and bad exceptions (vague, no ask)

process: An exception has four parts: what changed (the fact), what is affected (the impact), what is needed (the ask), and by when (the deadline).

Good exception: 'The vendor delayed the API delivery by 2 weeks (fact). This pushes the integration milestone past the launch date (impact). We need approval to either delay launch by 2 weeks or use the backup API at additional cost (ask) by Friday (deadline).'
Bad exception: 'There are some delays with the vendor.' This tells the reader nothing actionable: no impact assessment, no options, no deadline.
The test: after reading the exception, can the reader take action without asking follow-up questions? If not, the exception is incomplete.

steps.description: Define when a status report becomes an escalation and how the escalation path works.

inputs.name: report-structure
inputs.desc: The report template with status levels

outputs.name: escalation-rules
outputs.desc: When a yellow becomes a red, when a red triggers an out-of-cycle escalation, and who the escalation path reaches

outputs.name: escalation-templates
outputs.desc: Pre-written escalation messages for common scenarios: missed milestone, resource conflict, scope change, quality issue

process: Yellow to red: a yellow status becomes red when the issue has persisted for two reporting cycles without resolution, or when the impact exceeds a defined threshold (e.g., more than 1 week of delay, more than 10% cost overrun).
Red triggers escalation: when the status is red, an out-of-cycle escalation goes to the next level of decision-making within 24 hours. Do not wait for the next regular report.
Escalation path: define who receives escalations at each level. Level 1: the project owner. Level 2: the sponsor. Level 3: the executive team.

Pre-write the escalation templates. In a crisis, writing from scratch is slow. The template includes: what is the issue, what is the impact, what options are available, what is the recommendation, and what is the deadline for a decision.

description: Make meetings produce decisions, not discussions. Before: is a meeting the right tool? During: timeboxed agenda with named decision owners. After: decisions and actions sent within 24 hours. If a meeting does not produce a decision or an action, it should have been an email.

steps.description: Before scheduling: determine if a meeting is the right tool. Most meetings should be emails, documents, or async threads.

outputs.name: meeting-or-not
outputs.desc: Whether a meeting is the right tool (meeting) or not (email, document, async thread), with the reasoning

outputs.name: meeting-agenda
outputs.desc: If a meeting: the agenda with timeboxed items, decision owners, and pre-read materials. If not: the alternative action.

process: Apply the meeting filter: a meeting is justified when you need real-time interaction to reach a decision that cannot be reached asynchronously. This includes: resolving disagreements, brainstorming (not updates), making decisions where body language or tone matters, and handling sensitive topics.

A meeting is NOT justified for: sharing information (use a document), collecting status (use a form), approving routine decisions (use email), or working sessions where people work in parallel (use async with a sync check-in).

If the meeting is justified, write the agenda: each item has a time box (in minutes), a decision owner (the person who will make the call), and the pre-read (the information attendees need before the meeting, sent at least 24 hours in advance).
Invite only the people who must contribute to the decisions. Everyone else gets the meeting notes after.

steps.description: Run the meeting: start on time, follow the agenda, make decisions, capture actions.

inputs.name: meeting-agenda
inputs.desc: The timeboxed agenda with decision owners

outputs.name: meeting-execution-checklist
outputs.desc: The step-by-step protocol for running the meeting: open, discuss, decide, close, with timing

outputs.name: decision-capture-template
outputs.desc: The template for capturing decisions during the meeting: what was decided, by whom, and what actions follow

process: Start on time. Do not wait for latecomers. Do not recap for latecomers. This trains people to arrive on time.
For each agenda item: state the question to be decided, give the decision owner the floor, allow 80% of the time box for discussion, use the last 20% for the decision owner to make the call.
If a decision cannot be reached in the time box, the decision owner either extends (taking time from a later item) or moves the decision to async with a deadline.
Capture every decision and every action item in real time. An action item has: what, who, and by when. No action item is valid without all three.

steps.description: Send the decisions and actions within 24 hours. Track action completion. A meeting without follow-through is a social event.

inputs.name: decision-capture-template
inputs.desc: The decisions and actions captured during the meeting

inputs.name: participants
inputs.desc: The attendees plus anyone who needs to know

outputs.name: meeting-notes-template
outputs.desc: The notes format: decisions made, actions assigned (what, who, when), and next meeting date if needed. No transcript of the discussion.

outputs.name: action-tracking-setup
outputs.desc: How actions are tracked to completion: the tool, the check-in frequency, and the escalation path for overdue actions

process: Send the notes within 24 hours. The notes contain only: the decisions made and the actions assigned. They do not contain a transcript of who said what.
Each action item is tracked: the owner acknowledges receipt, provides status at the next check-in, and marks complete when done.

Overdue actions are escalated: if an action is not completed by its deadline, the meeting organizer follows up within 24 hours. If still not completed after 48 hours, it is escalated to the decision owner.
At the start of the next meeting, review the action items from the last meeting. This creates accountability and prevents actions from disappearing.

description: Pre-write crisis communication templates so that when a crisis hits, the response is fast, accurate, and consistent. Cover four scenarios: operational failure (outage, defect, delay), personnel issue (departure, misconduct), external event (market crash, regulation, competitor), and security incident (breach, data loss). For each: acknowledge, inform, act, follow up.

steps.description: Define the crisis scenarios your organization or household could face and categorize them by severity and audience.

inputs.name: stakeholder-groups
inputs.desc: The audiences that would need communication during a crisis (customers, employees, investors, media, family, neighbors)

outputs.name: crisis-scenarios
outputs.desc: The defined crisis scenarios with severity levels (minor, major, severe) and the primary affected audiences for each

outputs.name: response-time-targets
outputs.desc: For each scenario and severity: the target time for the first communication (minor: 24 hours, major: 4 hours, severe: 1 hour)

process: List the plausible crisis scenarios: service outage, product defect, key employee departure, security breach, data loss, legal action, negative media coverage, financial difficulty, natural disaster affecting operations.
For each scenario, define severity levels: minor (limited impact, quickly resolved), major (significant impact, extended resolution), severe (existential impact, fundamental response needed).
Map each scenario to its audiences: who needs to know, in what order, and how quickly?

Set the response time targets: the first communication must go out within the target window. Speed matters more than completeness. 'We are aware and investigating' within 1 hour beats a detailed report in 24 hours.

steps.description: Write the communication templates for each scenario and audience combination. Templates follow the AIAF pattern: Acknowledge, Inform, Act, Follow up.

inputs.name: crisis-scenarios
inputs.desc: The defined scenarios with severities and audiences

outputs.name: crisis-templates
outputs.desc: Pre-written templates for each scenario/audience combination: the AIAF structure with fill-in-the-blank specifics

outputs.name: do-not-say-list
outputs.desc: Phrases and commitments to avoid in crisis communication: speculation, blame, promises about timeline, minimization

process: For each template, use the AIAF structure. Acknowledge: 'We are aware of [specific issue].' Inform: 'Here is what we know so far: [facts only, no speculation].' Act: 'Here is what we are doing: [specific actions].' Follow up: 'We will provide the next update by [specific time].'

Write the templates with blanks for specifics. The structure stays the same; the details change. 'We are aware of [describe the issue]. As of [time], we know [confirmed facts]. We are [actions being taken]. We will update you by [next update time].'

Build the do-not-say list: never speculate ('We believe the cause might be...'), never blame ('This was caused by a vendor error'), never minimize ('Only a small number of users were affected' when you do not know the scope yet), never promise a timeline you cannot keep.
Create audience-specific versions: customers get impact and resolution timeline. Employees get internal actions and their role. Media gets a brief factual statement.

steps.description: Run a crisis communication drill: pick a scenario, execute the communication plan, and identify the gaps.

outputs.name: drill-results
outputs.desc: What worked (templates were found quickly, communication went out on time), what failed (wrong contact list, template did not fit the scenario, approval took too long), and the fixes

outputs.name: updated-playbook
outputs.desc: The revised crisis communication playbook incorporating the drill findings

process: Pick a scenario at random. Announce it to the team. Start the clock.

Execute the communication plan: find the template, fill in the blanks, get approval from the designated approver, and send to the designated audience. Measure the time from scenario announcement to first communication sent.
After the drill, review: was the template found quickly? Did it fit the scenario? Was the contact list current? Did the approval process cause delay? Was the communication clear and accurate?
Update the playbook with the findings. Schedule the next drill (semi-annually). Store the playbook where the team can find it during an actual crisis.

description: Transfer knowledge from one person (or team) to another without losing the tacit knowledge that lives in experience, judgment, and muscle memory. Documented procedures capture the what. Knowledge transfer captures the why, the exceptions, the judgment calls, and the patterns that only come from doing the work. Uses the apprenticeship model: observe, assist, perform, teach.

steps.description: Inventory the knowledge to be transferred: explicit knowledge (documented procedures) and tacit knowledge (judgment, exceptions, patterns).

inputs.name: knowledge-holder
inputs.desc: The person or team transferring knowledge (their role, tenure, and area of expertise)

inputs.name: knowledge-receiver
inputs.desc: The person or team receiving knowledge (their current skill level and learning style)

outputs.name: explicit-knowledge-list
outputs.desc: Documented procedures, guides, and references that already exist

outputs.name: tacit-knowledge-list
outputs.desc: The judgment calls, exceptions, patterns, and undocumented expertise that exist only in the knowledge holder's head

process: List the explicit knowledge: what is documented? Where is it? Is it current? Explicit knowledge is the easy part: hand over the documents.

Interview the knowledge holder to surface tacit knowledge. Ask: 'What do you know that is not written down anywhere?' 'What are the exceptions to the documented procedures?' 'When do you override the standard process, and why?' 'What are the three things that would take a new person the longest to figure out?'

Categorize the tacit knowledge: decision-making judgment (when to deviate from the standard), relationship knowledge (who to call for what), pattern recognition (what signals indicate a problem before it manifests), and workarounds (undocumented solutions to recurring issues).
Prioritize by criticality: which tacit knowledge, if lost, would cause the most damage? Transfer that first.

steps.description: Build the transfer schedule using the apprenticeship model: observe, assist, perform, teach. Each stage builds on the previous one.

inputs.name: tacit-knowledge-list
inputs.desc: The prioritized tacit knowledge to transfer

outputs.name: apprenticeship-schedule
outputs.desc: The stage-by-stage transfer plan: observe (watch the expert work and ask questions), assist (do the work with the expert present), perform (do the work independently with the expert available), teach (explain the work to someone else)

outputs.name: milestone-criteria
outputs.desc: How to know when the receiver is ready to move to the next stage

process: Stage 1 (Observe): the receiver watches the knowledge holder perform the work in real situations. The receiver asks questions and takes notes on the decisions, the exceptions, and the patterns. Duration: typically 1-2 weeks.
Stage 2 (Assist): the receiver performs parts of the work with the knowledge holder present and providing guidance. The knowledge holder corrects in real time. Duration: typically 2-4 weeks.

Stage 3 (Perform): the receiver performs the work independently. The knowledge holder is available for questions but does not intervene unless the receiver is about to make a significant error. Duration: typically 4-8 weeks.
Stage 4 (Teach): the receiver explains and demonstrates the work to a third person. Teaching is the strongest test of understanding. If the receiver can teach it, they own the knowledge.

steps.description: Run structured capture sessions to document the tacit knowledge as it is transferred. The goal is not perfect documentation but enough context that the receiver (or a future receiver) can reconstruct the judgment.

outputs.name: captured-knowledge-documents
outputs.desc: For each piece of tacit knowledge: the situation (when this knowledge applies), the judgment (what to do), the reasoning (why this is the right call), and the exceptions (when this judgment does not apply)

outputs.name: decision-playbooks
outputs.desc: Playbooks for the most critical judgment calls: 'When you see X, do Y, because Z. Unless W, then do V.'

process: Run capture sessions during stage 1 (Observe) and stage 2 (Assist). After each real-world situation, pause and document: what happened, what decision was made, why, and what alternatives were considered.

Use the format: Situation (when does this knowledge apply), Judgment (what to do), Reasoning (why this is correct), Exceptions (when this does not apply). This mirrors the SBI format but for knowledge instead of feedback.

For the most critical judgment calls, build decision playbooks: 'When you see [specific signal], do [specific action], because [specific reasoning]. Unless [specific exception], then do [alternative action].'

The documents are reference material, not replacements for the apprenticeship. Reading about judgment is not the same as developing judgment. The documents support the transfer; they do not replace it.

steps.description: Verify the transfer is complete. The knowledge holder should be able to step away without the operation degrading.

inputs.name: milestone-criteria
inputs.desc: The criteria for each apprenticeship stage

outputs.name: transfer-verification-results
outputs.desc: The test results: did the receiver handle real situations correctly without help? Were there knowledge gaps? What additional transfer is needed?

outputs.name: transfer-completion-record
outputs.desc: The complete record: what was transferred, how it was verified, what gaps remain, and the plan to address them

process: Test the transfer with real situations: the receiver handles a full cycle of work without the knowledge holder present. The knowledge holder reviews afterward.
Identify the gaps: which decisions did the receiver make differently than the knowledge holder would have? Were the differences improvements, neutral, or errors?
For errors, conduct a targeted transfer session on the specific knowledge gap. For improvements, update the documented knowledge.
The transfer is complete when the receiver can handle 90% of situations without assistance and knows when to escalate the remaining 10%.
